questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have family living close to Vancouver and wanted to live close to them.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit frustrating at times since the information came out pretty late so at times I would look for information without finding anything because the information was not out yet. But when the information did come out it was easy to find often found in email send directly to me.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Information sessions. You could also contact go global for further help.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There were a few information sessions I attended and they gave us resources to who we could contact if we needed more help. I never needed this help so I can not say if it is good or not.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were quite a few different buildings on campus you could choose between. Applying for all of them was done at the same time directly through UBC.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: As long as you did not live in first-year housing there was a shared kitchen for cooking. You could also choose to have a meal plan, I did not.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would definitely advise future students to apply for on-campus living. It does cost a bit of money to apply but it was very nice to live so close to classes and having roommates was a great way to meet new people. It is however a good idea to have a backup plan as on-campus living is not guaranteed for exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing available was nice (but a bit worn out) the only real problem is there is not enough so you can't be sure to be offered on campus-living.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was hard to find information about the different courses, often they only have a sentence or two to explain what they are. You also need to request quite a few more courses than you will have in the end and putting together so many courses that do not overlap is difficult. My advice for this would be not to worry too much you can change your courses once you have arrived, which also allows you to try out the course for a week or two. It is also possible to get into courses that have restrictions for exchange students if you speak to Go global/administration/the professor (depending on the course) after arriving.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You first send in a document of courses you would consider taking (this is not a registration but just to get into the university) around may you will then be sent a course registration survey which you fill out. You will need to request more courses than you will be registered in. The email with the survey will explain the details. Go Global will then look at the survey and register you for some of the courses you have requested. After arriving you can change the courses you are registered in.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can always contact Go Global, they usually answer fairly quickly and are helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got four courses I had wished for, they were 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th priorities. If I had wanted to I could have tried to get into my first priority after arriving but was pretty happy with the courses I had so didn't do that.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't panic, it's a bit overwhelming because there are so many courses with very little information about each and quite a few rules for what you can apply for. If in doubt contact Go Global at UBC they know all the details. If you don't get the courses you want definitely try contacting Go Global after you have arrived to hear if there is anything that can be done.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In general, the courses were well organized and interesting.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had three 3rd year courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The overall structure was similar to UCPH. All my courses had big lectures and two of them also had smaller classes that focused mostly on problem-solving. The grading however is quite a bit different. Rather than having one big final exam, you have lots of smaller assignments, quizzes, mid-terms, etc. on top of the final, these all count towards your final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MICB 302 Immunology
MICB 306 Molecular Virology
SCIE 300 Communicating Science

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All three that I had.
Immunology and molecular virology worked very well together as the topics overlap. They were also both interesting and built upon what I had previously learned in courses at UCPH but go into much more detail. They are definitely relevant to Molecular biomedicine students.
I also really enjoyed communicating science. It is a bit different from the others as it focuses more on group work than lectures. I think it is a good course as it gives you an introduction to writing both to a scientific audience (in the form of a scientific paper) as well as to a general audience (blog post, podcast, and video). The course also does not have any exams but instead assignments which I enjoyed.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I expected groceries to be about the same as in Denmark I was surprised to find it was more expensive. (A note to the numbers above, you could definitely live cheaper than I did, I went on quite a few trips, and in general, prioritized having a good time over saving money. The other fees are things like kitchen stuff, pillow, etc. which you need to get when you arrive)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Pretty much everything was more expensive. Groceries are a bit more expensive and definitely makes sense to go to a low-cost grocery store (I like No Frills). Public transport is cheaper since you have to get a U-pass through UBC, this coast 950 DKK for the whole semester. It allows you to with all public transport in metro Vancouver.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a bunch of clubs and other events at UBC, if you wanted to you could be busy every single day.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a club for just about everything. I would definitely recommend that you find one that fits your interests. There are options for lots of different sports, clubs for different religious believes, and various other hobbies.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The varsity outdoor club, VOC. It is one of the more expensive clubs but it gives you access to some awesome trips. If you like climbing I would also suggest the aviary, it's a climbing wall on UBC. You can learn to do climbing either through the VOC or the aviary if you don't know how already.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Try to get out of Vancouver too. Some recommendations I enjoyed: Bowen Island (a small island you can get to with the ferry great for a one-day hike), Vancouver Island (A big island, definitely recommend spending a couple of days here), Washington (Vancouver is really close to the US so a great opportunity to visit there as well I went to Seattle and the North Cascades National Park).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, honestly not much different from Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Getting to know local students is definitely harder than getting to know other exchange students. I would recommend joining clubs or putting effort into talking to the other students in your classes. Since there are so many exchange students who are all looking to meet new people it is easy to never really speak to anyone local if you don't make an effort to do so.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: As I said there really aren't too many differences but one thing I did find different was that casual hang-outs didn't seem to be as common, often you would have a concrete plan on what to do when meeting other people  (This might however just be because all the people were new to each other).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: In general, people were very kind and helpful.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Take time to enjoy non-academic opportunities, depending on which courses you choose, students are very motivated to do well (this seems to especially be the case if they want to go to medical school) and while studying is important, remember to take time to enjoy being in a whole new country.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are about a million different things for you to do, and you won't be able to do them all so choose the things you think you'll enjoy the most and take some time to relax as well.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know so many wonderful people and experiencing another culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being away from all the people you know best and trying to make new friends while getting used to a new country and new courses can be very hard.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Overall I loved going to UBC and living in Vancouver and would definitely recommend to other students.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
